newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - China SINOPEC's appeal for diesel imports cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - China SINOPEC's appeal for diesel imports cut.

text.p: A diesel glut in China has prompted state refiner Sinopec to lobby Beijing to keep second quarter imports down, industry sources said on Tuesday.
The government encouraged a surge in imports over the winter, but Sinopec has told it the move had led to oversupply in inland regions and pushed prices too low, they said.
"Refiners are not making any money at all because of the import glut," one refiner said.
Last month, Sinopec called for import licences to be held back in the first quarter to try to stop the build-up in stocks. It failed to sway Beijing, the sources said.

And to the dismay of Sinopec's 38 refineries, representing 80-percent of China's 4.3 million barrels per day (bpd) refining capacity, Beijing had yet to reply to the plea to moderate second quarter imports, the industry sources said.
Diesel imports have been volatile since late last year.

International prices rose to five-year highs last year, prompting China to rely heavily on its stocks. But, fearing they were falling too fast, the government encouraged imports and said up to one million tonnes of diesel imports were needed in January alone.

The sources said some two million tonnes may have been imported into China since the start of the year. At the same time, domestic production in January and February rose 9.3 percent and stocks were now ample and domestic prices falling.

"Domestic retail prices for diesel in Shenzhen have fallen by more than 100 yuan (US$12) to around 2,130-2,150 per tonne," said one refiner. "Prices have even fallen below the state set ex-refinery price at 2,190 yuan."
Market sources said the fall had been compounded by a rise in crude prices, to which refineries were trying to adjust.
China raised domestic crude prices -- the price at which state refineries can buy crude from the government -- by 86.8 yuan per tonne on December 25.
"End users would rather buy the cheaper imported diesel than to pay at higher ex-refinery prices," said one refiner. "The competitive imports are really eating our market share."
A Chinese trader in Singapore blamed Beijing's unpredictable oil policies for SINOPEC's plight. "Domestic prices are fluctuating with Beijing's import polices," he said.
China's state planners allocated import licences for as much as seven million tonnes of diesel in 1996, although only 4.6 million tonnes were actually imported.
"These refiners were already plagued by employing too many people, they are overtstaffed and are burdened with lifelong welfare and employment for its employees," the Chinese trader said.
SINOPEC pre-tax profits fell to 31.5 billion yuan in 1996, down 2.2 billion yuan from 1995.
But Chinese oil traders said they were not sympathetic to SINOPEC's blues. "We are still importing, although not in big volumes," said an official in Hong Kong with state trader SINOCHEM.
"While the Singapore benchmark diesel market is rampant with rumours of China limiting its imports, China is still buying as the coastal refineries start their refinery maintenance schedules."
US$1 = Yuan 8.3
-- Singapore newsroom (65-870-3082)
